Hi. I have about two minutes before my next meeting. What do you make?
Packaged foods, private label mostly. Before I take your two minutes — where are you based, and what do you buy?
Toronto. We are a distributor, so we buy and we sell on to about four hundred stores in Ontario.
And who do you buy this category from today?
Two suppliers, both in Europe. Prices went up twice last year, so I am here to look. Did you exhibit here last year?
No, we did not. This is our first year. Do you need a sample to take with you, or is the catalog more useful today?
Both, if you have them. And a price on twenty pallets, because that is what a first order looks like for us.
You will have it on Monday. One last question: who handles distribution decisions on your side, you or somebody above you?
I do, up to a point. Above a certain volume it goes to my director. Here is my badge — scan it, and follow up on Monday, not in three weeks.

Good morning, everybody, and welcome to day one. Two changes to the program before you go anywhere. First, the buyer meeting room has moved from hall two to hall four. Hall four, not hall two. Second, the panel on export rules now starts at eleven thirty, not at eleven, so you have half an hour more than you thought. Next, a reminder for the exhibitors. Every visitor badge here can be scanned at any booth. Please scan the badge instead of collecting business cards, because the contact details arrive already typed and you will not spend Friday night reading somebody's handwriting. And one piece of advice, from people who have done this for years. Do not close your booth early. The serious buyers walk the floor after four o'clock, when the crowd is gone and they can finally hear themselves think. The last hour is the best hour. Have a good show.

I have run a booth at about twenty of these, and I will tell you the one thing almost everybody gets wrong. They present. Somebody stops, and they talk about their own company for two minutes, beautifully, and at the end of those two minutes they know absolutely nothing about the person who was standing in front of them. And that person walks away and never comes back. My first two questions are always the same. Where are you based, and who do you buy this category from today. That is it. The first one tells me if they can even use what I sell, and the second one tells me whose business I would be taking, which is the only interesting question at a trade fair. And one last thing about leads, because people love to count them. Sixty leads that nobody follows up on are worth less than four that somebody actually calls on Monday morning. The fair is not the work. The Monday after it is the work.
